criteria.bounded_cascade: Same-transaction staged secondaries exactly as the flat rule, with one addition: a staged write landing on another model re-executes that model's create/update hooks within the same owner transaction, guarded by static cycle rejection plus a runtime depth bound, while any path back into the triggering CRUD stays forbidden. Current drafts cannot distinguish this from flat staging (no Transition/Notice hooks exist), so its only present effect is a larger promise for future composition. Price: cascade order, bound calibration, cross-model hook interplay, cross-model attribution, cascade/conflict test coverage and cascade-wide atomicity proof all become specified surface inside the bounded-work budget; debugging degrades because one staged line can pull foreign hooks into the user's commit, any of which may reject it; and no sampled draft workflow needs cascading, so the gain over explicit staging plus committed handlers is unproven while the surprise is certain.
criteria.committed_handlers: Restrict create/update hooks to the settled adjust-or-reject core and evict every secondary effect into committed-event handlers running as later, independently fenced transactions that cannot retroactively reject their sources. The safety surface is the smallest checkable one: a static ban on create/set/delete/schedule inside hook bodies, trigger rollback that can never strand staged writes because none exist, and no multi-row conflict surface. Price: trigger success plus handler failure is now a committed parent missing its children, owned by handler retry/recovery that has no dispatch evidence today; every one of the 36 secondary-effect hook bodies is remodeled with per-site re-proof; the deadline workflow must be re-demonstrated end to end across two transactions; and the drafts' staged, commonly-guarded intent is discarded without a concrete unsafety finding against staging itself.
criteria.declared_allowlist: Permit same-transaction staged secondaries only toward contract-declared targets — children parented to event.after and timers bound to the pending record — with flat evaluation, no cascading hooks, and A-style fencing, rollback and conflict handling over a statically auditable staged set. Undeclared staged writes fail at check time and reroute to committed handlers. Today's CanCheck secondaries all qualify, so no draft edits are needed now. Price: the allowlist's syntax, visibility and versioning are new language surface; each future hook relitigates whether its write counts as parented; authors learn two mechanisms plus the diagnostics that keep them apart; the boundary tracks syntax rather than a genuine trust or atomicity frontier, inviting re-parenting games, and cross-row needs discovered later push the list back toward the flat rule it was meant to avoid.
criteria.staged_flat: Authorize create/update hooks to stage secondary writes — other-row creates/writes, timer operations — that settle atomically with the triggering operation in a single owner transaction, re-running invariants and locks, reserving per-write versions, fencing every staged target's read revision, and evaluating the hook body once in written order with flat, non-cascading staging. Unsafe shapes stay rejected: no path into the triggering CRUD, no pending-source deletion, no delete-hook adjustment, no snapshot writes. Price: failure coupling is the sharp edge — a broad or contended staged write converts the user's simple update into a failed multi-row transaction with blame far from the cause; transactions, rechecks and attribution must fit the bounded-work budget; and single-owner atomicity for staged sets is specified but not yet engine-proven.

hook_rule.instructions: For the secondary-hook-write gate, which rule best preserves the five accepted workflows (pending adjustment with version fencing, staged children/timers or an adopted replacement, revision invalidation, atomic rollback, hook negatives), keeps genuinely unsafe hook behavior failing, and minimizes migration churn and semantic risk? Judge every option under the same workflow-preservation and minimal-intervention constraints.

request.state: The secondary-hook gate is a safety judgment first. Non-negotiable negatives: no hook may reenter its triggering CRUD path, delete its pending source, adjust from a delete hook, or mutate before/input snapshots; hook-observed revisions must conflict rather than silently authorize over concurrent change; trigger and staged effects must commit or roll back as one. The measured corpus behind the judgment: 44 CRUD hooks across 16 files (20 create, 23 update, 1 delete), of which 36 stage secondary effects — 17 parented children, 10 timers, 8 cross-row writes, 7 other — with zero delete attempts and 8 settled-only bodies. DESIGN settles the core both sides share: pre-commit adjust-or-reject hooks, no new client parameters, no callback into the triggering operation, one hook per model and operation, cycles as errors, version-1 rows in their creating transaction, v+1 reserved per accepted write, and no parent advancement from a child write; T30 provenance typing landed with spelling separated from semantics. Known unknowns that bound every option: R27's server-owned split between the rejecting update path and the accepting hook path with T18 offering no adopted rule; T28-A adopted for plain imports while T29 imported atomicity and split diagnostics remain owed; T16 done and T17a state-side landed against a durable plan that is still plan-not-proof with restarts unclaimed; one discriminating and one control example input with zero of 26 corpus blocks on hook scenarios and the R29 contract open; an R17 fencing residual wherever secrets are touched. The five accepted CanCheck workflows (pending adjustment with v/v+1 fencing, parented Transition/Notice staging, Deadline timer staging, invalidation, atomicity) must survive under whichever rule wins. This is a design choice, not a measured implementation result.
